<script type="application/json" id="pack-y1w02">{"year":1,"week":2,"id":"y1w02","title":"Properties of Operations and Sets","subtitle":"The closure, commutative, associative and distributive laws, identities and inverses — and the language of subsets, unions and intersections.","family":"number","section":{"no":1,"name":"Number","strand":"Number for Everyday Life","from":1,"to":8},"outcomes":["State and test the commutative, associative and distributive laws for real numbers.","Use a counterexample to show that a general statement is false.","Use identities, inverses and the distributive law to simplify and solve.","Use the words subset, union, intersection and complement, and draw simple Venn diagrams."],"keywords":["operation","property","closure","commutative","associative","distributive","identity","inverse","reciprocal","subset","union","intersection"],"notes":[{"title":"Operations and properties","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"An **operation** is a rule that combines two numbers to give a result. The four familiar operations are addition $(+)$, subtraction $(-)$, multiplication $(\\times)$ and division $(\\div)$."},{"k":"p","text":"A **property** is a general rule about an operation that is true for **every** allowed choice of numbers. Addition is an operation; the statement $a+b=b+a$ is a property of addition. Knowing the properties tells us when we may reorder, regroup or simplify a calculation without changing its value."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Closure and counterexamples","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Closure","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A set $S$ is **closed** under an operation $\\ast$ if, for every $a$ and $b$ in $S$, the result $a\\ast b$ is also in $S$."}]},{"k":"p","text":"Whole numbers are closed under $+$ and $\\times$ but not under $-$ or $\\div$. Integers are closed under $+$, $-$ and $\\times$. Rational and real numbers are closed under all four operations, provided we never divide by zero."},{"k":"p","text":"To show a set is **not** closed, name the set and find one pair whose result falls outside it. For $S=\\{1,2,3\\}$, even addition is not closed: $2+3=5\\notin S$. A small set does not inherit the closure of the integers."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"One counterexample is enough","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A single example that works does not prove a statement about every number. A single **counterexample** proves the statement false."}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"The commutative law — changing the order","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"For all real numbers $a$ and $b$:"},{"k":"math","tex":"a+b=b+a\\qquad\\text{and}\\qquad ab=ba"},{"k":"p","text":"For example, $14+26=26+14=40$ and $(-3)\\times8=8\\times(-3)=-24$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w02-arrays","caption":"Turning an array of 3 rows of 4 on its side gives 4 rows of 3: the total is 12 either way, so $3\\times4=4\\times3$."},{"k":"p","text":"Subtraction and division are **not** commutative: $8-3=5$ but $3-8=-5$; $12\\div3=4$ but $3\\div12=\\dfrac{1}{4}$. When you explain why a law fails, show both results."}],"figs":["w02-arrays"]},{"title":"The associative law — changing the grouping","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"For all real numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$:"},{"k":"math","tex":"(a+b)+c=a+(b+c)\\qquad\\text{and}\\qquad(ab)c=a(bc)"},{"k":"p","text":"The brackets move but the numbers stay in the same order. For example, $(20+35)+45=20+(35+45)=100$, and the second grouping is quicker because $35+45=80$."},{"k":"p","text":"Subtraction and division are **not** associative:"},{"k":"math","tex":"(12-5)-2=5\\quad\\text{but}\\quad 12-(5-2)=9"},{"k":"math","tex":"(24\\div6)\\div2=2\\quad\\text{but}\\quad 24\\div(6\\div2)=8"},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Do not mix up the two laws","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The **commutative** law changes the **order** of the numbers. The **associative** law changes only the **grouping** (the brackets)."}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"The distributive law","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Multiplication distributes over addition and subtraction:"},{"k":"math","tex":"a(b+c)=ab+ac\\qquad\\qquad a(b-c)=ab-ac"},{"k":"p","text":"Every term inside the bracket is multiplied by the factor outside: $4(3x-5)=12x-20$, **not** $12x-5$. A negative factor changes every sign: $-2(3x-7)=-6x+14$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w02-area","caption":"The area of the whole rectangle, $5(x+3)$, equals the sum of the two parts, $5x+15$."},{"k":"p","text":"**Factorising** reverses the distributive law: $18x+24=6(3x+4)$. It is useful for mental arithmetic, for example $25\\times48+25\\times52=25(48+52)=25\\times100=2500$."}],"figs":["w02-area"]},{"title":"Identity and inverse elements","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Identities and inverses","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["The **additive identity** is $0$, because $a+0=0+a=a$.","The **multiplicative identity** is $1$, because $a\\times1=1\\times a=a$.","The **additive inverse** of $a$ is $-a$, because $a+(-a)=0$.","The **multiplicative inverse** (reciprocal) of a non-zero number $a$ is $\\dfrac{1}{a}$, because $a\\times\\dfrac{1}{a}=1$."]}]},{"k":"p","text":"The additive inverse of $-\\dfrac{11}{5}$ is $\\dfrac{11}{5}$. The reciprocal of $-\\dfrac{4}{7}$ is $-\\dfrac{7}{4}$, because $\\left(-\\dfrac{4}{7}\\right)\\left(-\\dfrac{7}{4}\\right)=1$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w02-inverse","caption":"A number and its additive inverse are the same distance from 0 on opposite sides, so they add up to 0."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Zero has no reciprocal","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"There is no number $x$ with $0\\times x=1$, because $0\\times x$ is always $0$. That is why $\\dfrac{a}{b}$ is undefined when $b=0$."}]}],"figs":["w02-inverse"]},{"title":"Properties in algebra, and the language of sets","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The laws work together when we simplify. For $25(4x+3)-3(25x+2)$, expand each bracket and then regroup like terms:"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\begin{aligned}&25(4x+3)-3(25x+2)\\\\&=100x+75-75x-6\\\\&=(100x-75x)+(75-6)\\\\&=25x+69\\end{aligned}"},{"k":"p","text":"When solving, keep both sides balanced: from $3(x+2)=12$, divide **both** sides by 3 to get $x+2=4$, so $x=2$."},{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Set vocabulary","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["$A\\subseteq B$ ($A$ is a **subset** of $B$): every element of $A$ is also in $B$.","$A\\subset B$ ($A$ is a **proper subset** of $B$): $A\\subseteq B$ and $A\\neq B$.","$A\\cup B$ (**union**): elements in $A$ or in $B$ or in both.","$A\\cap B$ (**intersection**): elements in both $A$ and $B$.","$A'$ (**complement**, also written $A^{c}$): elements of the universal set $U$ that are not in $A$."]}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w02-subset","caption":"$A=\\{2,4\\}$ lies inside $B=\\{2,4,6\\}$, and $B$ has the extra element 6, so $A\\subset B$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w02-venn","caption":"Survey of Worked Example 2.6: the numbers show how many learners are in each region."},{"k":"p","text":"These ideas lead to the three-set problems of Week 3."}],"figs":["w02-subset","w02-venn"]}],"examples":[{"title":"Laws of addition in a bank calculation","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"An account manager receives GH₵125, GH₵375 and GH₵625 in one day. Show how the associative law makes the total easy to find, and explain why $125-375$ does not obey the commutative law."}],"steps":["The total is $125+375+625$.","Regroup using the associative law: $(125+375)+625=125+(375+625)$.","$375+625=1000$, so the total is $125+1000=1125$.","For subtraction, $125-375=-250$ but $375-125=250$. The results differ, so subtraction is not commutative."],"answer":"Total GH₵1 125; addition is associative, subtraction is not commutative.","figs":[]},{"title":"The distributive law in a stationery order","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A school buys 18 packs of exercise books. Each pack holds 12 ruled books and 8 unruled books. Use the distributive law to find the total number of books."}],"steps":["Each pack holds $(12+8)$ books, so the total is $18(12+8)$.","Distribute: $18\\times12+18\\times8=216+144=360$.","Check the other way: $18\\times20=360$ ✓."],"answer":"360 books","figs":[]},{"title":"Solving with a negative coefficient","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Solve $-3(2x-5)+4(x+2)=13$ and check your answer."}],"steps":["Expand: $-3(2x-5)=-6x+15$ and $4(x+2)=4x+8$.","Combine: $-6x+15+4x+8=13$, so $-2x+23=13$.","Subtract 23 from both sides: $-2x=-10$.","Divide both sides by $-2$: $x=5$.","Check: $-3(10-5)+4(5+2)=-15+28=13$ ✓."],"answer":"$x=5$","figs":[]},{"title":"Additive and multiplicative inverses","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"For $a=-\\dfrac{3}{8}$, find the additive inverse and the multiplicative inverse, and check each one."}],"steps":["Additive inverse: we need $b$ with $a+b=0$. Since $-\\dfrac{3}{8}+\\dfrac{3}{8}=0$, $b=\\dfrac{3}{8}$.","Multiplicative inverse: turn the fraction upside down and keep the sign: $c=-\\dfrac{8}{3}$.","Check: $\\left(-\\frac{3}{8}\\right)\\left(-\\frac{8}{3}\\right)=\\frac{24}{24}=1$"],"answer":"Additive inverse $\\dfrac{3}{8}$; multiplicative inverse $-\\dfrac{8}{3}$.","figs":[]},{"title":"Is division associative?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A learner says division is associative because $(64\\div8)\\div2$ and $64\\div(8\\div2)$ use the same three numbers. The order of the elements does not matter, and repeating an element does not change the set: $\\{2,2,4\\}=\\{2,4\\}$."},{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Key terms","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["The **universal set** $U$ is the whole group being studied, for example all the learners in a class.","The **empty set** $\\varnothing$ has no elements, so $n(\\varnothing)=0$.","The **cardinality** $n(A)$ is the number of distinct elements in $A$."]}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Union, intersection, difference and complement","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"For $A=\\{1,2,3\\}$ and $B=\\{3,4,5\\}$:"},{"k":"ul","items":["The **union** $A\\cup B=\\{1,2,3,4,5\\}$ contains the elements in $A$, in $B$ or in both. In mathematics “or” includes “both”.","The **intersection** $A\\cap B=\\{3\\}$ contains only the elements common to both sets.","The **difference** $A\\setminus B=\\{1,2\\}$ contains the elements of $A$ that are not in $B$. In general $A\\setminus B\\neq B\\setminus A$.","The **complement** $A'$ (also written $A^{c}$) contains the elements of $U$ that are not in $A$. Forgetting this correction is a common examination error."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Subsets and how many there are","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"If every element of $A$ is also in $B$, then $A$ is a **subset** of $B$, written $A\\subseteq B$. If also $A\\neq B$, then $A$ is a **proper subset**, written $A\\subset B$. For example $\\{4,6\\}\\subset\\{2,4,6\\}$, while $\\{2,4,6\\}$ is a subset of itself but not a proper subset."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Counting subsets","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The empty set is a subset of every set. An element in all three sets is counted three times at first, then subtracted three times with the pairs, leaving $0$. Adding $n(A\\cap B\\cap C)$ once restores its count to $1$. Read each phrase carefully: unless the word **only** is used, “learners taking Mathematics and ICT” includes those who also take Economics."},{"k":"fig","id":"w03-we1","caption":"The completed diagram for Worked Example 3.1. Find the number who study (i) only $M$, (ii) exactly two subjects, (iii) at least one subject, (iv) none of the subjects."}],"steps":["Centre: $n(M\\cap I\\cap E)=12$.","Two subjects only: $M\\cap I$ only $=30-12=18$; $M\\cap E$ only $=25-12=13$; $I\\cap E$ only $=20-12=8$.","One subject only: $M$ only $=70-18-13-12=27$; $I$ only $=55-18-8-12=17$; $E$ only $=48-13-8-12=15$.","Exactly two: $18+13+8=39$.","At least one: $27+17+15+18+13+8+12=110$.","None: $120-110=10$.","Check with inclusion–exclusion: $70+55+48-30-25-20+12=110$ ✓."],"answer":"(i) 27 (ii) 39 (iii) 110 (iv) 10","figs":[]},{"title":"A proper subset and its subsets","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Let $U=\\{1,2,3,4,5,6\\}$, $A=\\{2,4\\}$ and $B=\\{1,2,3,4\\}$. Is $A$ a proper subset of $B$? How many subsets does $A$ have? List them."}],"steps":["Both elements of $A$, $2$ and $4$, are in $B$, so $A\\subseteq B$.","$B$ also contains $1$ and $3$, so $A\\neq B$. Hence $A\\subset B$.","$A$ has 2 elements, so it has $2^2=4$ subsets.","They are $\\varnothing$, $\\{2\\}$, $\\{4\\}$ and $\\{2,4\\}$."],"answer":"Yes, $A\\subset B$; $A$ has 4 subsets: $\\varnothing$, $\\{2\\}$, $\\{4\\}$, $\\{2,4\\}$.","figs":[]},{"title":"Using the three-set formula","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Among 90 learners, 40 prefer football $(F)$, 38 basketball $(B)$ and 35 athletics $(A)$. 14 prefer football and basketball, 13 football and athletics, and 11 basketball and athletics; 5 prefer all three. How many prefer none of the three?"}],"steps":["Substitute into the formula: $\\begin{aligned}&n(F\\cup B\\cup A)\\\\&=40+38+35-14-13-11+5\\end{aligned}$","Add the single totals: $40+38+35=113$.","Subtract the pairs: $113-14-13-11=75$.","Add back the triple: $75+5=80$.","None: $90-80=10$."],"answer":"10 learners","figs":[]},{"title":"Exactly one and exactly two","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"For three clubs, $n(A)=36$, $n(B)=29$, $n(C)=31$, $n(A\\cap B)=12$, $n(A\\cap C)=14$, $n(B\\cap C)=10$ and $n(A\\cap B\\cap C)=4$. Find how many learners join exactly one club and exactly two clubs."}],"steps":["Two clubs only: $A\\cap B$ only $=12-4=8$; $A\\cap C$ only $=14-4=10$; $B\\cap C$ only $=10-4=6$.","One club only: $A$ only $=36-8-10-4=14$; $B$ only $=29-8-6-4=11$; $C$ only $=31-10-6-4=11$.","Exactly one: $14+11+11=36$. Exactly two: $8+10+6=24$.","Check: $36+24+4=64$, and $36+29+31-12-14-10+4=64$ ✓."],"answer":"Exactly one: 36; exactly two: 24.","figs":[]},{"title":"Verifying De Morgan’s law by listing","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Let $U=\\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8\\}$, $A=\\{1,2,3,5\\}$ and $B=\\{3,4,5,7\\}$. Show that $(A\\cup B)'=A'\\cap B'$."}],"steps":["$A\\cup B=\\{1,2,3,4,5,7\\}$, so $(A\\cup B)'=\\{6,8\\}$.","$A'=\\{4,6,7,8\\}$ and $B'=\\{1,2,6,8\\}$.","$A'\\cap B'=\\{6,8\\}$.","Both sides give the same set."],"answer":"$(A\\cup B)'=A'\\cap B'=\\{6,8\\}$","figs":[]},{"title":"Interpreting De Morgan’s law for three sets","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"In a school, $A$, $B$ and $C$ are the sets of learners taking Agriculture, Biology and Chemistry. Describe $(A\\cup B\\cup C)'$ in words and explain why it equals $A'\\cap B'\\cap C'$."}],"steps":["$A\\cup B\\cup C$ is everyone taking at least one of the three subjects.","Its complement is everyone taking **none** of them.","To take none, a learner must be outside $A$ **and** outside $B$ **and** outside $C$.","“And” means intersection, so this set is $A'\\cap B'\\cap C'$."],"answer":"Both describe the learners who take none of Agriculture, Biology or Chemistry.","figs":[]},{"title":"A survey with all regions given","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A school surveyed 150 learners about three clubs. 40 joined $A$ only, 25 joined $B$ only, 20 joined $C$ only; 15 joined $A$ and $B$ only, 10 joined $A$ and $C$ only, 12 joined $B$ and $C$ only, and 8 joined all three. How many joined no club?"}],"steps":["These seven regions do not overlap, so add them.","One club only: $40+25+20=85$. Two clubs only: $15+10+12=37$.","Inside the circles: $85+37+8=130$.","No club: $150-130=20$. All eight regions now total 150 and none is negative ✓."],"answer":"20 learners","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results for Week 3","items":["A set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets and $2^n-1$ proper subsets.","$n(A\\cup B)=n(A)+n(B)-n(A\\cap B)$","$n(A\\cup B\\cup C)=n(A)+n(B)+n(C)-n(A\\cap B)-n(A\\cap C)-n(B\\cap C)+n(A\\cap B\\cap C)$","$(A\\cup B)'=A'\\cap B'$ and $(A\\cap B)'=A'\\cup B'$","“None” $=n(U)-n(A\\cup B\\cup C)$"]}],"quiz":[{"q":"If $A=\\{1,2\\}$ and $B=\\{1,2,3\\}$, which statement must be true?","options":["$A=B$","$B\\subset A$","$A\\subset B$","$A\\cap B=\\varnothing$"],"correct":2,"explain":"Every element of $A$ is in $B$, and $B$ has the extra element $3$, so $A$ is a proper subset of $B$."},{"q":"For $A=\\{1,3,5\\}$ and $B=\\{3,4,5\\}$, $A\\cap B$ is","options":["$\\{3,5\\}$","$\\{1,3,4,5\\}$","$\\{1,4\\}$","$\\varnothing$"],"correct":0,"explain":"The intersection contains only the elements in both sets: $3$ and $5$."},{"q":"A set with 4 elements has how many subsets?","options":["$4$","$8$","$12$","$16$"],"correct":3,"explain":"A set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets: $2^4=16$."},{"q":"Which expression is equal to $(A\\cup B\\cup C)'$?","options":["$A'\\cup B'\\cup C'$","$A'\\cap B'\\cap C'$","$A\\cap B\\cap C$","$A'\\cap(B\\cup C)$"],"correct":1,"explain":"De Morgan’s law takes the complement of every set and changes the union into an intersection."},{"q":"In a survey, $n(A)=30$, $n(B)=25$ and $n(A\\cap B)=12$. Find $n(A\\cup B)$.","options":["$67$","$43$","$55$","$13$"],"correct":1,"explain":"$n(A\\cup B)=30+25-12=43$."},{"q":"9 learners join all three clubs and 22 join both $A$ and $B$. How many are in $A$ and $B$ only?","options":["$31$","$22$","$9$","$13$"],"correct":3,"explain":"$n(A\\cap B)$ includes the 9 in all three clubs, so $A\\cap B$ only $=22-9=13$."},{"q":"The set $A\\setminus B$ contains the elements","options":["in $A$ but not in $B$","in either $A$ or $B$","in both $A$ and $B$","outside both $A$ and $B$"],"correct":0,"explain":"The difference $A\\setminus B$ keeps the elements of $A$ that are not in $B$."},{"q":"Three sets have sizes 30, 27 and 25; their pairwise intersections have sizes 8, 9 and 7, and the triple intersection has size 3. The union has size","options":["$61$","$58$","$64$","$76$"],"correct":0,"explain":"$30+27+25-8-9-7+3=82-24+3=61$."},{"q":"Which description means “in exactly two of $A$, $B$ and $C$”?","options":["$(A\\cup B\\cup C)'$","$A\\cap B\\cap C$","the three “two sets only” regions together","$A\\cup B\\cup C$"],"correct":2,"explain":"Exactly two means in two sets but not the third: the $A\\cap B$ only, $A\\cap C$ only and $B\\cap C$ only regions."},{"q":"$U$ has 80 members and $n(A\\cup B\\cup C)=68$. How many members are in none of the sets?","options":["$148$","$68$","$12$","$0$"],"correct":2,"explain":"None $=n(U)-n(A\\cup B\\cup C)=80-68=12$."}],"exercise":[{"q":"For $U=\\{1,2,\\ldots,12\\}$, $A=\\{2,4,6,8,10,12\\}$ and $B=\\{3,6,9,12\\}$, find $A\\cup B$, $A\\cap B$, $A'$ and $B'$.","a":"$A\\cup B=\\{2,3,4,6,8,9,10,12\\}$; $A\\cap B=\\{6,12\\}$; $A'=\\{1,3,5,7,9,11\\}$; $B'=\\{1,2,4,5,7,8,10,11\\}$."},{"q":"180 learners were asked about French, ICT and Economics: 90, 75 and 65 take them; 35 take French and ICT, 30 French and Economics, 25 ICT and Economics; 15 take all three. Find how many take exactly one, exactly two, at least one, and none.","a":"Exactly one 95, exactly two 45, at least one 155, none 25."},{"q":"Explain, in words, why $(A\\cup B\\cup C)'=A'\\cap B'\\cap C'$.","a":"An element outside $A\\cup B\\cup C$ is in none of the sets, so it is outside $A$, outside $B$ and outside $C$ — that is, in $A'\\cap B'\\cap C'$; the reverse is also true."},{"q":"A three-set Venn diagram has 6 in the centre, 7, 9 and 11 in the “two sets only” regions, and 14, 18 and 12 in the “one set only” regions. Find $n(A\\cup B\\cup C)$.","a":"$6+27+44=77$"},{"q":"How many proper subsets does a set with five elements have? Why is this one fewer than the number of subsets?","a":"$2^5-1=31$; the only subset that is not proper is the set itself."},{"q":"$n(A)=12$, $n(B)=9$ and $n(A\\cup B)=17$. Find $n(A\\cap B)$.","a":"$12+9-17=4$"},{"q":"List all the subsets of $\\{p,q,r\\}$.","a":"$\\varnothing$, $\\{p\\}$, $\\{q\\}$, $\\{r\\}$, $\\{p,q\\}$, $\\{p,r\\}$, $\\{q,r\\}$, $\\{p,q,r\\}$ — 8 subsets."},{"q":"In a group of 60 people, 35 like tea, 30 like coffee and 12 like both. How many like neither?","a":"$35+30-12=53$ like at least one, so $60-53=7$ like neither."}],"theory":[{"q":"Out of 100 learners, 52 take French $(F)$, 46 take ICT $(I)$ and 35 take Economics $(E)$; 20 take $F$ and $I$, 17 take $F$ and $E$, 14 take $I$ and $E$, and 7 take all three. Find all eight regions of the Venn diagram.","steps":["Centre: 7.","$F\\cap I$ only $=20-7=13$; $F\\cap E$ only $=17-7=10$; $I\\cap E$ only $=14-7=7$.","$F$ only $=52-13-10-7=22$; $I$ only $=46-13-7-7=19$; $E$ only $=35-10-7-7=11$.","Union $=22+19+11+13+10+7+7=89$; none $=100-89=11$."],"answer":"22, 19, 11, 13, 10, 7, 7 inside the circles and 11 outside.","model":null},{"q":"Let $U=\\{a,b,c,d,e,f\\}$, $A=\\{a,b,d\\}$ and $B=\\{b,c,f\\}$. Find $(A\\cup B)'$ and $A'\\cap B'$, and comment.","steps":["$A\\cup B=\\{a,b,c,d,f\\}$, so $(A\\cup B)'=\\{e\\}$.","$A'=\\{c,e,f\\}$ and $B'=\\{a,d,e\\}$, so $A'\\cap B'=\\{e\\}$.","The two sets are equal, as De Morgan’s law states."],"answer":"Both equal $\\{e\\}$.","model":null},{"q":"A survey reports 20 in $A$ only, 25 in $B$ only, 15 in $C$ only, 10 in $A\\cap B$ only, 6 in $A\\cap C$ only, 9 in $B\\cap C$ only and 5 in all three. How many chose exactly one, exactly two and at least two?","steps":["Exactly one: $20+25+15=60$.","Exactly two: $10+6+9=25$.","At least two: $25+5=30$."],"answer":"60, 25 and 30.","model":null},{"q":"Find the number of subsets and of proper subsets of a set with 6 elements. Explain the role of the empty set.","steps":["Each element is either included or not: $2^6=64$ subsets.","Only the set itself is not a proper subset: $64-1=63$ proper subsets.","The empty set is one of the 64 subsets, and it is a proper subset because the set is not empty."],"answer":"64 subsets and 63 proper subsets.","model":null},{"q":"Explain the three-set inclusion–exclusion formula, and why the triple intersection is added back after the pairs are subtracted.","steps":["Adding $n(A)+n(B)+n(C)$ counts an element in two sets twice and an element in three sets three times.","Subtracting the three pairwise intersections corrects the double counts, but an element in all three sets is subtracted three times, leaving a count of $3-3=0$.","Adding $n(A\\cap B\\cap C)$ once restores that element to a count of 1."],"answer":"Every element ends up counted exactly once.","model":null}],"checklist":["I can tell a subset from a proper subset and count subsets with $2^n$.","I can find unions, intersections, differences and complements.","I can fill in all eight regions of a three-set Venn diagram.","I can use the inclusion–exclusion formula for two and three sets.","I can state and check De Morgan’s laws."],"plan":{"lessons":[[{"j":0,"notes":true,"exs":[]},{"j":1,"notes":true,"exs":[0]},{"j":2,"notes":true,"exs":[1]},{"j":3,"notes":true,"exs":[]}],[{"j":4,"notes":true,"exs":[2,3]},{"j":5,"notes":true,"exs":[4,5]},{"j":6,"notes":true,"exs":[6]}]],"exSec":[1,2,4,4,5,5,6],"quizSec":[2,1,2,5,5,3,1,1,3,3],"exerSec":[5,4,3,3,2,5,2,1],"thSec":[3,1,4,2,4],"sumSec":[2,5,5,5,3],"chkSec":[2,1,3,4,5],"weights":[590.6,1486.4,1491.5,1262.1,2079.15,2294.9,1187],"figs":[{"id":"w03-subsets","sec":2,"lesson":1,"caption":"The set $\\{a,b,c\\}$ has $2^3=8$ subsets, including $\\varnothing$ and the set itself."},{"id":"w03-demorgan","sec":5,"lesson":2,"caption":"Shading the complement of the union leaves only the outside region; <script type="application/json" id="pack-y1w04">{"year":1,"week":4,"id":"y1w04","title":"Understanding and Representing Fractions","subtitle":"Parts of a whole, equivalent fractions, comparing and ordering, mixed numbers, why the four operations work, and fractions as decimals.","family":"number","section":{"no":1,"name":"Number","strand":"Number for Everyday Life","from":1,"to":8},"outcomes":["Explain a fraction as part of a whole, part of a set, a point on the number line and a division.","Identify proper, improper, unit, like, unlike and equivalent fractions and mixed numbers.","Simplify fractions and compare or order them without a calculator.","Explain and use the rules for adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing fractions.","Decide whether a fraction gives a terminating or a recurring decimal."],"keywords":["numerator","denominator","equivalent fraction","lowest terms","mixed number","improper fraction","common denominator","reciprocal","terminating decimal","recurring decimal"],"notes":[{"title":"What a fraction really means","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A fraction is a **single number**, not just two numbers written one above the other. In $\\dfrac{3}{5}$ the **denominator** $5$ tells us that one whole has been cut into five **equal** parts, and the **numerator** $3$ tells us that three of those parts are taken."},{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Numerator and denominator","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"In the fraction $\\dfrac{a}{b}$ (with $b\\neq0$), the denominator $b$ names the size of the parts (fifths, eighths, …) and the numerator $a$ counts how many of those parts we have."}]},{"k":"p","text":"The same fraction can describe four different situations. If three of five identical bottles are full, $\\dfrac{3}{5}$ of the bottles are full. If three loaves are shared equally by five people, each person gets $3\\div5=\\dfrac{3}{5}$ of a loaf."},{"k":"fig","id":"w04-meanings","caption":"Four meanings of $\\frac{3}{5}$: part of a whole, part of a set, a point on the number line, and the result of $3\\div5$."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"The parts must be equal","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Three pieces out of five **unequal** pieces are not $\\dfrac{3}{5}$ of the whole. Before you write a fraction, check that the whole has been cut into equal parts."}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w04-unequal","caption":"Counting pieces is not enough when the pieces have different sizes."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Zero and the denominator","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["$\\dfrac{0}{7}=0$, because zero parts of anything is nothing.","A denominator can **never** be $0$: $\\dfrac{7}{0}$ would mean $7\\div0$, which is undefined.","Fractions can be negative: $-\\dfrac{3}{7}=\\dfrac{-3}{7}=\\dfrac{3}{-7}$."]}]}],"figs":["w04-meanings","w04-unequal"]},{"title":"Fraction strips and benchmark fractions","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"**Fraction strips** are bars of the same length, each cut into equal parts. Because every strip represents the same whole, you can compare fractions by comparing the shaded lengths."},{"k":"fig","id":"w04-strips","caption":"All three strips have the same length, and the shaded part is exactly half of each one: $\\frac{1}{2}=\\frac{2}{4}=\\frac{3}{6}$."},{"k":"p","text":"On a number line, equal distances must represent equal amounts. The **benchmark fractions** $0$, $\\dfrac{1}{4}$, $\\dfrac{1}{2}$, $\\dfrac{3}{4}$ and $1$ are useful reference points. For example, $\\dfrac{7}{15}$ is a little less than $\\dfrac{1}{2}$, because half of $15$ is $7.5$ and $7<7.5$."},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"Quick test against one half","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A positive fraction $\\dfrac{a}{b}$ is less than $\\dfrac{1}{2}$ when $2a<b$, equal to $\\dfrac{1}{2}$ when $2a=b$, and greater than $\\dfrac{1}{2}$ when $2a>b$. So $\\dfrac{9}{16}>\\dfrac{1}{2}$ because $18>16$."}]}],"figs":["w04-strips"]},{"title":"Types of fractions","blocks":[{"k":"table","head":["Type","Meaning","Example"],"rows":[["Proper","numerator less than denominator","$\\dfrac{5}{8}$"],["Improper","numerator equal to or greater than denominator","$\\dfrac{13}{8}$"],["Mixed number","a whole number and a proper fraction","$1\\dfrac{5}{8}$"],["Unit","numerator $1$","$\\dfrac{1}{12}$"],["Like","same denominator","$\\dfrac{3}{11}$, $\\dfrac{8}{11}$"],["Unlike","different denominators","$\\dfrac{3}{8}$, $\\dfrac{5}{12}$"],["Equivalent","different forms of the same number","$\\dfrac{2}{3}=\\dfrac{8}{12}$"]]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Equivalent fractions and lowest terms","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Multiplying or dividing the numerator **and** the denominator by the same non-zero number does not change the value of a fraction, because you are multiplying by $\\dfrac{k}{k}=1$."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Equivalent fractions","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"\\frac{a}{b}=\\frac{a\\times k}{b\\times k}=\\frac{a\\div k}{b\\div k}\\qquad(b\\neq0,\\ k\\neq0)"}]},{"k":"p","text":"For example, $\\dfrac{2}{3}=\\dfrac{2\\times4}{3\\times4}=\\dfrac{8}{12}$."},{"k":"p","text":"A fraction is in its **lowest terms** (simplest form) when the highest common factor (HCF) of the numerator and denominator is $1$. To simplify $\\dfrac{84}{126}$, find $\\text{HCF}(84,126)=42$ and divide both terms by $42$:"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\frac{84}{126}=\\frac{84\\div42}{126\\div42}=\\frac{2}{3}"},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Change both terms, never just one","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Dividing only the numerator, or only the denominator, changes the value of the fraction. Also, you may not add the same number to both terms: $\\dfrac{1}{2}\\neq\\dfrac{1+1}{2+1}=\\dfrac{2}{3}$."}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Comparing and ordering fractions","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Same denominator:** compare the numerators. $\\dfrac{3}{11}<\\dfrac{8}{11}$.","**Same numerator:** the larger denominator gives smaller parts. $\\dfrac{3}{8}<\\dfrac{3}{5}$.","**Unlike fractions:** rewrite them over a **common denominator**, preferably the lowest common multiple (LCM) of the denominators.","**Cross-multiplication:** for positive $b$ and $d$, $\\dfrac{a}{b}<\\dfrac{c}{d}$ exactly when $ad<bc$. State that the denominators are positive when you use this shortcut."]},{"k":"fig","id":"w04-numberline","caption":"The fractions $\\frac{7}{12}$, $\\frac{11}{18}$ and $\\frac{5}{8}$ are very close together; over the common denominator 72 their order is clear."}],"figs":["w04-numberline"]},{"title":"Mixed numbers and improper fractions","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"To change a mixed number into an improper fraction, multiply the whole number by the denominator and add the numerator."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Converting mixed numbers","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"w\\frac{a}{b}=\\frac{w\\times b+a}{b}"},{"k":"p","text":"Here $w\\dfrac{a}{b}$ means $w+\\dfrac{a}{b}$, the whole number $w$ plus the fraction $\\dfrac{a}{b}$."}]},{"k":"p","text":"For example, $2\\dfrac{3}{7}=\\dfrac{2\\times7+3}{7}=\\dfrac{17}{7}$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w04-mixed","caption":"Three wholes are eighteen sixths, and five more sixths make twenty-three sixths."},{"k":"p","text":"To change an improper fraction into a mixed number, divide: the quotient is the whole number and the remainder is the new numerator. For $\\dfrac{29}{6}$: $29\\div6=4$ remainder $5$, so $\\dfrac{29}{6}=4\\dfrac{5}{6}$."}],"figs":["w04-mixed"]},{"title":"The four operations: why the rules work","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"**Adding and subtracting.** You can only combine parts of the same size, so the fractions need a common denominator first. Then add or subtract the numerators and keep the denominator."},{"k":"math","tex":"\\frac{2}{9}+\\frac{4}{9}=\\frac{6}{9}=\\frac{2}{3}"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\frac{1}{3}+\\frac{1}{4}=\\frac{4}{12}+\\frac{3}{12}=\\frac{7}{12}"},{"k":"fig","id":"w04-add","caption":"Thirds and quarters are different-sized parts. Cutting both into twelfths makes them the same size, so they can be added."},{"k":"p","text":"**Multiplying.** The word “of” usually means multiply. $\\dfrac{2}{3}$ of $\\dfrac{3}{5}$ is"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\frac{2}{3}\\times\\frac{3}{5}=\\frac{2\\times3}{3\\times5}=\\frac{6}{15}=\\frac{2}{5}"},{"k":"fig","id":"w04-multiply","caption":"Taking $\\frac{2}{3}$ of the $\\frac{3}{5}$ strip gives 6 of the 15 equal cells, which is $\\frac{2}{5}$ of the whole."},{"k":"p","text":"**Dividing.** $6\\div\\dfrac{1}{2}$ asks “how many halves are in $6$?” The answer is $12=6\\times2$. In the same way, dividing by a non-zero fraction is the same as multiplying by its **reciprocal**:"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\frac{3}{4}\\div\\frac{2}{5}=\\frac{3}{4}\\times\\frac{5}{2}=\\frac{15}{8}=1\\frac{7}{8}"},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"The four operations","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["$\\dfrac{a}{c}+\\dfrac{b}{c}=\\dfrac{a+b}{c}$ and $\\dfrac{a}{c}-\\dfrac{b}{c}=\\dfrac{a-b}{c}$","$\\dfrac{a}{b}\\times\\dfrac{c}{d}=\\dfrac{ac}{bd}$","$\\dfrac{a}{b}\\div\\dfrac{c}{d}=\\dfrac{a}{b}\\times\\dfrac{d}{c}=\\dfrac{ad}{bc}$ $\\;(c\\neq0)$"]}]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Common mistakes","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["$\\dfrac{1}{3}+\\dfrac{1}{4}\\neq\\dfrac{2}{7}$. Never add the denominators.","In division, turn over only the fraction you are dividing **by**, not the first fraction.","Change mixed numbers into improper fractions before multiplying or dividing."]}]}],"figs":["w04-add","w04-multiply"]},{"title":"Fractions and decimals","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"To write a fraction as a decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator: $\\dfrac{3}{8}=3\\div8=0.375$. The decimal either stops (**terminates**) or repeats forever (**recurs**)."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Which fractions terminate?","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A fraction in its **lowest terms** has a terminating decimal exactly when its denominator has no prime factors other than $2$ and $5$."},{"k":"ul","items":["$\\dfrac{7}{40}$ terminates because $40=2^3\\times5$: $\\dfrac{7}{40}=0.175$.","$\\dfrac{2}{7}$ recurs because $7$ is a prime other than $2$ or $5$: $\\dfrac{2}{7}=0.\\dot{2}8571\\dot{4}$."]}]},{"k":"table","head":["Fraction","Decimal","Fraction","Decimal"],"rows":[["$\\dfrac{1}{2}$","$0.5$","$\\dfrac{1}{8}$","$0.125$"],["$\\dfrac{1}{4}$","$0.25$","$\\dfrac{1}{3}$","$0.\\dot{3}$"],["$\\dfrac{3}{4}$","$0.75$","$\\dfrac{2}{3}$","$0.\\dot{6}$"],["$\\dfrac{1}{5}$","$0.2$","$\\dfrac{1}{6}$","$0.1\\dot{6}$"]]},{"k":"p","text":"A dot over a digit shows that it repeats; dots over the first and last digits show a repeating block. Writing a number as a decimal does not change its value."},{"k":"box","kind":"life","title":"Fractions around us","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Market traders sell “half a bag” or “a quarter of a tin”; recipes use $\\dfrac{3}{4}$ cup of flour; a lorry may be $\\dfrac{2}{3}$ full of cocoa; and a football match has two halves of 45 minutes."}]}],"figs":[]}],"examples":[{"title":"Fraction of a farm","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A farmer divided a plot of land into 24 equal sections and planted maize on 15 of them. Find the fraction planted with maize in its lowest terms, and the fraction not yet planted."}],"steps":["There are 24 equal sections and 15 are planted, so the fraction planted is $\\dfrac{15}{24}$.","$\\text{HCF}(15,24)=3$, so $\\frac{15}{24}=\\frac{15\\div3}{24\\div3}=\\frac{5}{8}$","Unplanted sections: $24-15=9$, so the unplanted fraction is $\\dfrac{9}{24}$, which simplifies to $\\dfrac{3}{8}$.","Check: $\\dfrac{5}{8}+\\dfrac{3}{8}=\\dfrac{8}{8}=1$ whole ✓."],"answer":"Planted: $\\dfrac{5}{8}$; not planted: $\\dfrac{3}{8}$.","figs":[]},{"title":"Ordering close fractions","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Without a calculator, arrange $\\dfrac{7}{12}$, $\\dfrac{5}{8}$ and $\\dfrac{11}{18}$ in ascending order. Use a common denominator."}],"steps":["The denominators are $12=2^2\\times3$, $8=2^3$ and $18=2\\times3^2$, so $\\text{LCM}=2^3\\times3^2=72$.","$\\dfrac{7}{12}=\\dfrac{42}{72}$, $\\quad\\dfrac{5}{8}=\\dfrac{45}{72}$, $\\quad\\dfrac{11}{18}=\\dfrac{44}{72}$.","Since $42<44<45$, the fractions are in the same order."],"answer":"$\\dfrac{7}{12}<\\dfrac{11}{18}<\\dfrac{5}{8}$","figs":[]},{"title":"Filling small containers","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A container holds $3\\dfrac{5}{6}$ litres of oil. Write this as an improper fraction, and find how many containers of $\\dfrac{1}{6}$ litre each can be completely filled."}],"steps":["$3\\dfrac{5}{6}=\\dfrac{3\\times6+5}{6}=\\dfrac{23}{6}$ litres.","Number of small containers $=$ total volume $\\div$ volume of one container.","$\\dfrac{23}{6}\\div\\dfrac{1}{6}=\\dfrac{23}{6}\\times\\dfrac{6}{1}=23$.","This makes sense: there are 23 sixths of a litre, and each container takes one sixth."],"answer":"$\\dfrac{23}{6}$ litres; 23 containers.","figs":[]},{"title":"Are these fractions different?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A pupil claims that $\\dfrac{14}{21}$ and $\\dfrac{26}{39}$ are different amounts because their numerators are different. Assess the claim."}],"steps":["$\\text{HCF}(14,21)=7$, so $\\dfrac{14}{21}=\\dfrac{2}{3}$.","$\\text{HCF}(26,39)=13$, so $\\dfrac{26}{39}=\\dfrac{2}{3}$.","Both fractions reduce to $\\dfrac{2}{3}$, so they are equivalent.","Check by cross-multiplication: $14\\times39=546$ and $21\\times26=546$ ✓."],"answer":"The claim is false: both fractions equal $\\dfrac{2}{3}$.","figs":[]},{"title":"Which club used more?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Two clubs each received an identical packet of materials. Club A used $\\dfrac{3}{5}$ of its packet and Club B used $\\dfrac{7}{12}$ of its packet. Which club used more, and by what fraction of a packet?"}],"steps":["$\\text{LCM}(5,12)=60$.","Club A: $\\dfrac{3}{5}=\\dfrac{36}{60}$. Club B: $\\dfrac{7}{12}=\\dfrac{35}{60}$.","$\\dfrac{36}{60}>\\dfrac{35}{60}$, so Club A used more.","Difference: $\\dfrac{36}{60}-\\dfrac{35}{60}=\\dfrac{1}{60}$."],"answer":"Club A, by $\\dfrac{1}{60}$ of a packet.","figs":[]},{"title":"Filling a tank","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A tank is $\\dfrac{2}{5}$ full. Water equal to $\\dfrac{1}{4}$ of the tank’s capacity is added. What fraction of the tank is now full? Does it overflow?"}],"steps":["Both fractions are parts of the same full tank, so they can be added.","$\\text{LCM}(5,4)=20$: $\\dfrac{2}{5}=\\dfrac{8}{20}$ and $\\dfrac{1}{4}=\\dfrac{5}{20}$.","$\\dfrac{8}{20}+\\dfrac{5}{20}=\\dfrac{13}{20}$.","$\\dfrac{13}{20}<1$, so the tank does not overflow."],"answer":"$\\dfrac{13}{20}$ full; no overflow.","figs":[]},{"title":"Sharing a sample","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"In a laboratory, $\\dfrac{3}{4}$ of a sample is shared equally among five test tubes. What fraction of the whole sample is in each tube?"}],"steps":["Sharing equally among 5 means dividing by 5: $\\dfrac{3}{4}\\div5$.","Write $5=\\dfrac{5}{1}$; its reciprocal is $\\dfrac{1}{5}$.","$\\dfrac{3}{4}\\times\\dfrac{1}{5}=\\dfrac{3}{20}$.","Check: $5\\times\\dfrac{3}{20}=\\dfrac{15}{20}=\\dfrac{3}{4}$ ✓."],"answer":"$\\dfrac{3}{20}$ of the sample","figs":[]},{"title":"Terminating or recurring?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Without dividing, decide whether $\\dfrac{9}{24}$ and $\\dfrac{5}{11}$ have terminating decimals.
